1: And every Jew needs to cherish Eretz Yisrael and come to it from the ends of the earth with great longing—like a child [running] to their mother’s embrace. For the root of our sin, which caused crying for generations, was that we despised it, as it says: “They rejected the desirable land” (Psalms 106:24). But in the redemption of our souls, may it soon, it is written: “For Thy servants hold her stones dear, and cherish her very dust” (Psalms 102:15), and there it says: “Thou wilt arise, and have mercy upon Zion” (Psalms 102:14). And therefore, the Amoraim would kiss its dust and its stones when they arrived there. And how good and how pleasant it is to sing a song of affection composed about it by Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi with great love—the beginning of the poem: “O holy land, precious and beloved,” etc. So too we sing by the memorial of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai every Rosh Chodesh eve with great joy, and we plead with God that He not send us out from upon it. Also those near and those far who are outside it should yearn and long for it, for just as God chose them, so too He chose Eretz Yisrael and designated it for them. And they are not called “one nation” except with it, as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explained the verse: “And who is like Your people Israel, one nation in the land” (I Samuel 7:23).

And we find in the Midrash that the Holy One, blessed be He, first told Avraham Avinu to go to Eretz Yisrael, and see it, and return. And after he returned, he was not permitted to go back for five years—and during those five years he longed intensely to go to return. And [about this] he said this verse: “Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then I would fly away, and be at rest. Lo, then I would wander far off, and remain in the wilderness. Sela.” (Psalms 55:7–8)—better to dwell in the deserts of Eretz Yisrael than in the palaces of the Diaspora.And he was longing, and when he was permitted [to go] it is written “So Avram departed, as Hashem had spoken to him” (Genesis 12:4). Before he came to the land, he did not yet long for it—but after he came once and saw, through prophetic vision, the precious beauty of its holiness, he yearned for it deeply. From him we learn for all generations—we, his descendants—that we too should long as he did, even though its inhabitants suffer; for that reason, we should accept suffering with joy.
